answer.answer: Scrapy defaults TWISTED_REACTOR to 'twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor' so that asyncio is supported natively: asyncio and asyncio-powered libraries can be used in any coroutine, and new projects need no additional setup (recorded as the accepted decision 'asyncio reactor by default', from docs/topics/asyncio.rst). The default is set in scrapy/settings/default_settings.py (module scrapy.settings.default_settings), line 609. With CrawlerRunner/AsyncCrawlerRunner the reactor must still be installed manually via scrapy.utils.reactor.install_reactor.

The default TWISTED_REACTOR is twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor because that reactor is what turns on Scrapy's native asyncio support. With it you can use asyncio and asyncio-powered libraries in any coroutine (callbacks, start(), and so on). History: Scrapy 2.7.0 made new projects from startproject use this reactor by default. Scrapy 2.13.0 then changed the setting's own default from None to the asyncio reactor, so existing projects that don't set it explicitly also get the asyncio reactor. Projects can still switch to a different reactor if needed. The default is set in scrapy/settings/default_settings.py at line 609, next to TWISTED_REACTOR_ENABLED = True. The repository does not give any deeper design rationale beyond enabling asyncio support and aligning existing projects with new ones.

Scrapy defaults TWISTED_REACTOR to twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor so that asyncio support is enabled out of the box: asyncio and asyncio-powered libraries can be used in any coroutine, and new projects need no additional setup (decision:asyncio-reactor-default, from docs/topics/asyncio.rst:7-27). The default is set in scrapy/settings/default_settings.py (module scrapy.settings.default_settings), line 609: TWISTED_REACTOR = "twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor". With AsyncCrawlerRunner/CrawlerRunner the reactor must still be installed manually via scrapy.utils.reactor.install_reactor.

docs/topics/item-pipeline.rst ("Item Pipeline", section "Writing your own item pipeline") explains how to write an item pipeline component. It says each component must implement process_item(self, item), which must return an item or raise DropItem, and may also implement open_spider(self), called when the spider is opened (it may raise CloseSpider), and close_spider(self), called when the spider is closed before the spider_closed signal. Any of these may be coroutine functions (async def).

The file docs/topics/item-pipeline.rst explains this in its section "Writing your own item pipeline". It says every item pipeline component must implement process_item(self, item). That method must either return an item object or raise DropItem. A component may also implement open_spider(self), which is called when the spider opens and may raise CloseSpider, and close_spider(self), which is called when the spider closes, before the spider_closed signal is sent. Any of these methods may be defined as a coroutine. The examples further down the file also use the from_crawler classmethod that components can define.

The default request fingerprinter is the RequestFingerprinter class (docstring: "Default fingerprinter."), defined in the scrapy.utils.request module (scrapy/utils/request.py). Its fingerprint() method delegates to scrapy.utils.request.fingerprint, which hashes the canonicalized URL, method and body with SHA1.

By default Scrapy computes request fingerprints with the RequestFingerprinter class, set by the REQUEST_FINGERPRINTER_CLASS default setting to 'scrapy.utils.request.RequestFingerprinter'. It is defined in the scrapy.utils.request module. Its docstring calls it the 'Default fingerprinter'; its fingerprint() method delegates to the module-level fingerprint() function, which hashes the canonical URL, method and body with SHA1. The crawler loads the class from that setting.

By default Scrapy computes request fingerprints with the RequestFingerprinter class: the REQUEST_FINGERPRINTER_CLASS setting defaults to "scrapy.utils.request.RequestFingerprinter", and the crawler loads it with load_object. The class is defined in the scrapy.utils.request module.

The retry downloader middleware is RetryMiddleware, implemented in the module scrapy.downloadermiddlewares.retry (scrapy/downloadermiddlewares/retry.py). Its __init__ raises NotConfigured unless the RETRY_ENABLED setting is true, and reads RETRY_TIMES as the maximum number of retries (max_retry_times). A request's meta key max_retry_times can override it. Related settings it reads are RETRY_HTTP_CODES, RETRY_PRIORITY_ADJUST, RETRY_GIVE_UP_LOG_LEVEL and RETRY_EXCEPTIONS.

The retry downloader middleware is RetryMiddleware in the module scrapy.downloadermiddlewares.retry. It is turned on by the RETRY_ENABLED setting (the constructor raises NotConfigured when it is false; default True) and the number of retries is set by RETRY_TIMES (default 2, i.e. initial response plus 2 retries), which can be overridden per request with the max_retry_times meta key.

The retry downloader middleware is RetryMiddleware in the module scrapy.downloadermiddlewares.retry. It is turned on by the RETRY_ENABLED setting (default True; the middleware raises NotConfigured if it is false), and RETRY_TIMES sets how many times a failed request is retried (default 2, i.e. initial response + 2 retries).

The graph does not give a fixed requests-per-second figure. Scrapy's defaults don't set a rate at all. They cap concurrency: CONCURRENT_REQUESTS = 16 overall and CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 8. DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 0, so there is no delay between requests, and AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED = False. The real throughput therefore depends on server latency and response times, not on a configured requests/second value.

Scrapy's defaults do not set a fixed requests-per-second rate. The rate depends on how fast servers respond, and it is capped by concurrency: CONCURRENT_REQUESTS = 16 overall and CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 8, with DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 0 (no wait between requests) and AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED = False. So with the built-in defaults you get up to 16 requests in flight at once (8 per domain), not a set number per second. A project generated by `startproject` overrides this in its settings template (CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 1, DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 1), which the docs describe as about one request per second per domain.

The repository does not define a fixed requests-per-second rate for default settings. So the actual requests per second depends on server response latency and isn't a configured number; the files show no explicit requests-per-second value.

The repository does not establish whether scrapy.core.scheduler.Scheduler is thread-safe. Its docstring (scrapy/core/scheduler.py:127-251) and docs/topics/scheduler.rst describe priority queues, request order, JOBDIR persistence and duplicate filtering, but say nothing about threads or thread safety, and the class body (lines 252-498) contains no thread, lock or other synchronization references. The only related statement is architectural: Scrapy is built on Twisted and uses non-blocking asynchronous code for concurrency instead of threads (docs/topics/architecture.rst:151-156), which implies single-threaded use within the reactor but is not a thread-safety guarantee for the Scheduler.

Its docstring and method docs (enqueue_request, next_request, open, close) say nothing about threads or thread safety, and the module imports no locking or threading primitives. enqueue_request and next_request change the dupefilter, the priority queues and stats with no synchronization. A search of the repository for 'thread-safe'/'threadsafe' finds only asyncio call_soon_threadsafe/run_coroutine_threadsafe uses in crawler.py and shell.py, none about the scheduler. The 'Concurrency affects order' section covers concurrent requests (CONCURRENT_REQUESTS) and request order, not thread safety. So no thread-safety guarantee is documented, and none is ruled out either.
